instance_group [ { count: 2, kind: KIND_GPU, gpus: [ 0 ] } ]

qs.q: Why decode RTSP video on the GPU with NVDEC instead of on the CPU? Walk through a zero-copy decode-to-inference pipeline.
qs.a:
The PCIe arithmetic decides it. A 1080p RGB frame is 1920 × 1080 × 3 = 6.2 MB. 300 cameras at 25 fps is 7,500 frames/s, or 46.7 GB/s of raw pixels if you decode on CPU and upload. A PCIe Gen4 x16 link carries about 32 GB/s per direction. The compressed H.264/H.265 stream is a few Mbit/s per camera, so you ship the bitstream to the GPU and decode there.

NVDEC is a fixed-function decoder block separate from the SMs, so decoding does not steal CUDA cores from inference. Its throughput is per-GPU and per-codec; check NVIDIA's Video Codec SDK performance tables for the card you own and measure it.

Pipeline:

  1. Demux RTSP (FFmpeg/GStreamer), keep packets on CPU. They are small.
  2. NVDEC decodes into NV12 surfaces in device memory (1920 × 1080 × 1.5 = 3.1 MB per frame).
  3. One CUDA kernel does NV12 to RGB, letterbox resize and normalisation straight into the TensorRT input buffer.
  4. TensorRT runs on the same stream; only boxes (a few KB) return to the host.

Gotchas:

  • You cannot skip decoding P-frames: they reference earlier frames. Running inference at 5 fps still means decoding all 25. To cut decode cost, decode only keyframes (I-frames) when 1 fps per GOP is enough.
  • Frame pool memory: 4 NV12 buffers per stream × 300 streams × 3.1 MB ≈ 3.7 GB of VRAM before any model loads.
  • RTSP over UDP drops packets and produces grey smeared frames; use TCP interleaved transport, and detect and drop corrupted frames.
  • Tools: DeepStream (nvv4l2decoder), FFmpeg with -hwaccel cuda, or NVIDIA's Python video codec bindings.

qs.q: Build the latency budget for a camera alert: event happens on the road, alert reaches the operator. Where does the time go and what do you control?
qs.a:
Break the chain into stages and measure each with timestamps carried through the pipeline (camera PTS, receive time, decode done, inference done, alert emitted):

  • Camera encode + network + RTSP jitter buffer: often the largest fixed cost; measure glass-to-glass with a clock in view of the camera.
  • Decode: NVDEC, usually small but it grows with GOP structure and queueing.
  • Queue + batching delay: up to max_queue_delay plus waiting behind other cameras.
  • Inference + NMS + tracking: the part people optimise, often not the largest.
  • Decision logic: temporal debounce. Requiring 5 consecutive frames at 5 fps adds 5 × 200 ms = 1 s by construction.
  • Alert delivery: message queue, network, UI.

What you control: the debounce window (trade false alerts against latency explicitly), inference fps per camera, batch delay, and queue policy.

Overload policy matters more than mean latency. Bound every per-camera queue and drop the oldest frame, never the newest, so the system degrades to lower fps instead of rising lag. Monitor frame age at inference time (now minus capture timestamp) per camera; a rising age is the earliest sign of overload, and it shows up before the GPU looks saturated.

Fairness: round-robin across cameras when forming batches so one busy camera cannot starve the others.

qs.q: nvidia-smi shows 100% GPU utilization but throughput is far below what trtexec measured. How do you profile the pipeline?
qs.a:
First, what the number means: nvidia-smi "GPU-Util" is the percentage of time in the sample window that at least one kernel was running. A single tiny kernel running all the time reads 100% while most SMs sit idle. Use DCGM profiling metrics (SM active, SM occupancy, tensor pipe active) for real utilisation.

Then get a timeline: nsys profile the serving process for a few seconds under load and look for:

  • Gaps between kernels: the GPU waits on the CPU. Typical causes: Python preprocessing (cv2 resize, numpy normalisation), the GIL, per-frame small kernel launches.
  • Synchronous memcpy from pageable memory: copies stall the stream. Use pinned host buffers and cudaMemcpyAsync on a non-default stream.
  • Everything on one stream: copy, preprocess and inference serialise. Use separate streams or multiple Triton instances so copies overlap compute.
  • Small batches: trtexec measured batch 16; production sends batch 1-2 because the client is synchronous.
  • Post-processing on CPU: decode boxes and NMS in Python per frame.

Method: measure stage throughput in isolation (decode only, preprocess only, engine only with trtexec, end to end). The slowest stage is the ceiling; optimise that one, re-measure, repeat. The goal is end-to-end frames/s close to the engine-only number.

qs.q: Implement softmax with numerical stability.
qs.a: Subtract max before exponentiation to prevent overflow. This doesn't change the result (exp(x-c)/Σexp(xi-c) = exp(x)/Σexp(xi)).

qs.q: Implement cross-entropy loss and its gradient.
qs.a: Cross-entropy loss for multi-class classification. Gradient is beautifully clean: predictions minus one-hot labels.
qs.code:
import numpy as np

def cross_entropy_loss(logits, labels):
    """
    logits: (batch, n_classes)
    labels: (batch,) integer class indices
    """
    probs = softmax(logits)
    n = logits.shape[0]
    # select log-prob of correct class for each example
    loss = -np.log(probs[np.arange(n), labels] + 1e-9)
    return loss.mean()

def cross_entropy_grad(logits, labels):
    """Returns dL/d_logits. Shape: (batch, n_classes)"""
    probs = softmax(logits)
    n = logits.shape[0]
    probs[np.arange(n), labels] -= 1  # subtract 1 for correct class
    return probs / n

qs.q: Implement a 2-layer MLP forward and backward pass in pure NumPy.
qs.a: Core exercise in understanding backprop. Store activations in forward pass, reuse in backward.
qs.code:
import numpy as np

class MLP:
    def __init__(self, d_in, d_h, d_out, lr=0.01):
        # He initialization for ReLU
        self.W1 = np.random.randn(d_in, d_h) * np.sqrt(2 / d_in)
        self.b1 = np.zeros(d_h)
        self.W2 = np.random.randn(d_h, d_out) * np.sqrt(2 / d_h)
        self.b2 = np.zeros(d_out)
        self.lr = lr

    def relu(self, x): return np.maximum(0, x)

    def forward(self, x):
        self.x = x
        self.z1 = x @ self.W1 + self.b1
        self.a1 = self.relu(self.z1)
        self.z2 = self.a1 @ self.W2 + self.b2
        return self.z2  # logits

    def backward(self, dL_dz2):
        """dL_dz2: gradient of loss w.r.t. output logits, shape (batch, d_out)"""
        self.dW2 = self.a1.T @ dL_dz2         # (d_h, d_out)
        self.db2 = dL_dz2.sum(0)              # (d_out,)
        dL_da1 = dL_dz2 @ self.W2.T           # (batch, d_h)
        dL_dz1 = dL_da1 * (self.z1 > 0)       # ReLU grad
        self.dW1 = self.x.T @ dL_dz1          # (d_in, d_h)
        self.db1 = dL_dz1.sum(0)              # (d_h,)

    def step(self):
        self.W1 -= self.lr * self.dW1
        self.b1 -= self.lr * self.db1
        self.W2 -= self.lr * self.dW2
        self.b2 -= self.lr * self.db2

qs.q: Implement K-Means clustering with K-Means++ initialization.
qs.a: K-Means++ initialization spreads initial centers proportional to squared distance, avoiding poor local minima.
qs.code:
import numpy as np

def kmeans(X, k, n_iter=100, seed=42):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n = len(X)

    # K-Means++ initialization
    centers = [X[rng.integers(n)]]
    for _ in range(k - 1):
        dists = np.array([min(np.sum((x - c)**2) for c in centers) for x in X])
        probs = dists / dists.sum()
        centers.append(X[rng.choice(n, p=probs)])
    centers = np.array(centers)

    for _ in range(n_iter):
        # Assign: (n, k) squared distances
        dists = np.sum((X[:, None] - centers[None])**2, axis=-1)
        labels = dists.argmin(axis=1)

        # Update centers
        new_centers = np.array([
            X[labels == j].mean(0) if (labels == j).any() else centers[j]
            for j in range(k)
        ])
        if np.allclose(centers, new_centers, atol=1e-6):
            break
        centers = new_centers

    inertia = sum(np.sum((X[labels == j] - centers[j])**2) for j in range(k))
    return centers, labels, inertia

qs.q: Implement precision, recall, F1, and BLEU score from scratch.
qs.a: These metrics come up in both classification and NLP evaluation questions.
qs.code:
import numpy as np
from collections import Counter

def classification_metrics(y_true, y_pred):
    tp = np.sum((y_pred == 1) & (y_true == 1))
    fp = np.sum((y_pred == 1) & (y_true == 0))
    fn = np.sum((y_pred == 0) & (y_true == 1))
    precision = tp / (tp + fp + 1e-9)
    recall    = tp / (tp + fn + 1e-9)
    f1 = 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall + 1e-9)
    return {"precision": precision, "recall": recall, "f1": f1}

def bleu_score(reference, hypothesis, max_n=4):
    """Simplified BLEU for a single reference."""
    import math
    ref_tokens = reference.split()
    hyp_tokens = hypothesis.split()

    # Brevity penalty
    bp = 1.0 if len(hyp_tokens) >= len(ref_tokens) else \
         math.exp(1 - len(ref_tokens) / len(hyp_tokens))

    log_score = 0
    for n in range(1, max_n + 1):
        ref_ngrams = Counter(
            tuple(ref_tokens[i:i+n]) for i in range(len(ref_tokens) - n + 1))
        hyp_ngrams = Counter(
            tuple(hyp_tokens[i:i+n]) for i in range(len(hyp_tokens) - n + 1))
        clipped = sum(min(count, ref_ngrams[gram])
                      for gram, count in hyp_ngrams.items())
        total = max(len(hyp_tokens) - n + 1, 1)
        log_score += math.log(clipped / total + 1e-9) / max_n

    return bp * math.exp(log_score)

qs.q: Implement IoU and greedy NMS in NumPy, plus class-aware (batched) NMS.
qs.a:
IoU = intersection area / union area. Vectorise as an (N, M) matrix with broadcasting.

Greedy NMS: sort by score; take the top box; drop every remaining box with IoU above the threshold; repeat. Worst case O(N²).

Class-aware NMS without a loop over classes: offset each box by class_id × (max coordinate + 1) so boxes of different classes can never overlap, then run one NMS. torchvision's batched_nms uses the same trick.

Follow-ups to expect: why NMS breaks in crowds (two overlapping true objects, one gets suppressed; Soft-NMS decays scores instead of deleting), and why NMS-free detectors (DETR, YOLOv10) need one-to-one assignment during training.
qs.code:
import numpy as np

def iou_matrix(a, b):
    """a: (N,4), b: (M,4) boxes as x1,y1,x2,y2. Returns (N,M) IoU."""
    x1 = np.maximum(a[:, None, 0], b[None, :, 0])
    y1 = np.maximum(a[:, None, 1], b[None, :, 1])
    x2 = np.minimum(a[:, None, 2], b[None, :, 2])
    y2 = np.minimum(a[:, None, 3], b[None, :, 3])
    inter = np.clip(x2 - x1, 0, None) * np.clip(y2 - y1, 0, None)
    area_a = (a[:, 2] - a[:, 0]) * (a[:, 3] - a[:, 1])
    area_b = (b[:, 2] - b[:, 0]) * (b[:, 3] - b[:, 1])
    return inter / (area_a[:, None] + area_b[None, :] - inter + 1e-9)

def nms(boxes, scores, iou_thr=0.5):
    """Greedy NMS. Returns indices of kept boxes, highest score first."""
    order = np.argsort(-scores)
    keep = []
    while order.size > 0:
        i = order[0]
        keep.append(int(i))
        if order.size == 1:
            break
        ious = iou_matrix(boxes[i:i + 1], boxes[order[1:]])[0]
        order = order[1:][ious <= iou_thr]
    return keep

def batched_nms(boxes, scores, classes, iou_thr=0.5):
    """Class-aware NMS via the offset trick: shift each class far apart."""
    offset = classes[:, None] * (boxes.max() + 1)
    return nms(boxes + offset, scores, iou_thr)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    b = np.array([[0, 0, 10, 10], [1, 1, 11, 11], [20, 20, 30, 30], [0, 0, 10, 10]], float)
    s = np.array([0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6])
    c = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1])
    print(nms(b, s))              # [0, 2]: box 1 and box 3 overlap box 0
    print(batched_nms(b, s, c))   # [0, 2, 3]: box 3 is a different class
    # 8x8 box shifted by 2 px -> IoU 0.6
    print(iou_matrix(np.array([[0, 0, 8, 8.]]), np.array([[2, 0, 10, 8.]])))

qs.q: Implement Average Precision for one class from scratch (score sorting, greedy matching, PR envelope).
qs.a:
Steps:

  1. Sort all predictions for the class across all images by score, descending.
  2. Walk the list. A prediction is a TP if its best-IoU ground truth in the same image is above the threshold and not already matched; otherwise FP. Duplicates of an already-matched object are FPs.
  3. Cumulative TP and FP give precision and recall at every rank.
  4. Make precision monotone (precision at recall r = max precision at any recall ≥ r), then integrate over recall.

Variants: VOC 2007 sampled 11 recall points; later VOC uses all points (this code); COCO samples 101 recall points and averages over IoU 0.50:0.05:0.95 and over classes.

Check in the demo: ranks TP, TP, FP, TP with 3 GT give AP = 2/3 × 1 + 1/3 × 0.75 = 0.9167.

qs.q: Tell me about a challenging ML project and what you learned.
qs.a:
Structure: STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result)

What interviewers look for:

  • Clear problem definition - did you understand the real problem before building?
  • Data thinking - what were the data challenges? How did you handle distribution issues?
  • Iteration mindset - what didn't work and why? How did you debug?
  • Quantifiable impact - accuracy improved X%, latency reduced Y%
  • Honest self-assessment - what would you do differently?

interview angle: lead with my CV production work. Pick one project - object detection or a model serving challenge - and tell it with specific technical details (what backbone, what loss, what data augmentation strategy, what evaluation metrics).

Avoid: vague descriptions, no numbers, blaming external factors, no reflection.

qs.q: How do you stay current with ML research?
qs.a:
Frontier labs want specifics, not "I follow arXiv."

Good answers include:

  • arXiv daily: cs.LG, cs.CV, cs.CL - subscribe to feeds, use Semantic Scholar
  • Papers you've read recently: be specific (name the paper, why it interested you, key insight)
  • Twitter/X follows: @karpathy, @ylecun, @sama, @hardmaru, @ilyasut
  • Blogs: Lilian Weng (lilianweng.github.io), Sebastian Raschka, The Gradient
  • Podcasts: Dwarkesh Patel, Lex Fridman, Machine Learning Street Talk
  • Code: re-implement interesting papers in PyTorch (this teaches more than just reading)

Tip: before the interview, read 2-3 recent papers relevant to the company's work. Have a concrete opinion on each. "I read the Flash Attention 3 paper last week and found the warp specialization insight fascinating because..." is a much stronger answer than "I follow arXiv."

qs.q: A model worked great in testing but failed in production. Walk me through the debugging.
qs.a:
This is a classic ML system debugging question. Interviewers want systematic thinking.

Common causes + checks:

  • Data leakage: did features in test set contain future information? Check feature timestamps vs label timestamps.
  • Distribution mismatch: is production data distribution similar to test set? Compare feature distributions. Did anything change after data collection?
  • Preprocessing bugs: is the production preprocessing pipeline identical to training? Missing normalization? Different tokenizer version?
  • Batch norm inference mode: is model in eval mode? (Dropout + BatchNorm behave differently at inference)
  • Feature drift: are the features being computed correctly? Log some production inputs and compare to training examples.
  • Label delay: if labels come with delay, the validation might have been evaluated with delayed labels that aren't available in production.

Process: 1) Reproduce the failure offline with a production input. 2) Shadow mode test (log but don't serve production predictions). 3) Compare data distributions. 4) Check every step of the pipeline.

qs.q: How do you approach a project with very limited labeled data?
qs.a:
• Transfer learning: fine-tune a pretrained model (CLIP, DINOv2 for CV; BERT/GPT for NLP). Often works with 100-1000 labeled examples.
  • Self-supervised pretraining: if you have unlabeled data in-domain, pretrain on it (MAE, contrastive learning) before fine-tuning on the small labeled set.
  • Data augmentation: for CV: random crop, flip, color jitter, mixup. For NLP: back-translation, synonym replacement, EDA.
  • Active learning: query a model to label the most informative unlabeled examples first. Uncertainty sampling, core-set selection, query-by-committee.
  • Semi-supervised learning: use unlabeled data with pseudo-labels (FixMatch, MixMatch). Train on labeled + predicted-label unlabeled examples.
  • Weak supervision (Snorkel): write labeling functions (heuristics, regex, knowledge bases) to programmatically label unlabeled data. Combine with denoising model.
  • Synthetic data: generate training examples with LLMs (text), or with GANs/diffusion (images).

qs.q: How do you debug a model with a flat loss curve?
qs.a:
Systematic debugging process for training issues:

  1. Verify data pipeline first: print a batch. Is it the same every iteration (forgot to shuffle)? Are labels correct? Are inputs in expected range?
  2. Check learning rate: too low → flat loss. Too high → NaN or exploding loss. Try 10× higher, then 10× lower.
  3. Verify loss computation: is reduction correct (mean vs sum)? Is loss actually being backpropagated (no .detach() accidentally on the right variable)?
  4. Check gradient flow: print gradient norms per layer. If all zeros, something is wrong in the graph. If all NaN, exploding gradients.
  5. Overfit a single batch: train on 1 batch for 100 steps. If loss doesn't reach near-zero, there's a fundamental bug. Loss should be -log(1/n_classes) ≈ 2.3 initially for 10-class.
  6. Check initialization: initial loss should be close to -log(1/n_classes). If very different, initialization or loss formula is wrong.

If a single batch will not overfit: forgot optimizer.zero_grad() (gradients accumulate); off-by-one between inputs and targets; probabilities fed into a loss that expects logits; model left in eval mode; a different batch each step. A model can memorize 32 examples, so failure means a wiring bug, not a learning problem.

qs.q: How do you explain AI limitations to a non-technical PM who wants 99% accuracy?
qs.a:
This is a communication + technical maturity question.

Framework:

  • Ground with the baseline: "The current rule-based system achieves X%. No model achieves 99% on this kind of data."
  • Explain irreducible error: "Some inputs are inherently ambiguous - even humans disagree. Our target can't exceed human-level performance on ambiguous cases."
  • Reframe the metric: "99% overall accuracy may not be the right goal. If Type II errors (missed fraud) cost 10× more than Type I, we should optimize that, not accuracy."
  • Set expectations with data: "SOTA for this task is 93%. We can realistically target 88-90% at launch."

interview angle: my experience teaching AI to seniors makes me well-suited for this. Draw on how you explain model limitations in InterviewReady.

qs.q: How do you decide whether a problem needs ML at all?
qs.a:
Strong candidates know ML is not always the answer.

Don't use ML when:

  • Rule-based logic handles it fully (route emails by subject line)
  • Insufficient data (<1000 labeled examples for a complex task)
  • Interpretability is legally required (regulated credit or medical decisions)
  • Latency constraint makes inference infeasible (<1ms requirement)
  • Training cost exceeds value (one-time task, simple pattern)

Use ML when: patterns are too complex for hand-crafted rules, sufficient labeled data exists, prediction errors are acceptable, the task generalizes across many inputs.

Rule: always baseline with a simple heuristic first. If the rule gets 90%, the ML bar is 95%+ with acceptable cost and complexity. The delta must justify the complexity.

qs.q: Tell me about a time you improved model performance significantly.
qs.a:
Structure: what was the baseline, what did you try, what worked, what did you measure, what was the outcome?

Strong signals interviewers look for:

  • You measured first (profiled, identified bottleneck) rather than guessing
  • You tried multiple hypotheses systematically, not randomly
  • You can explain WHY something worked, not just that it worked
  • You have specific numbers (mAP went from 0.76 to 0.91, not "significantly improved")

My story: the 54% latency reduction at Beltech via NMS-free YOLOv10 + TensorRT is a strong story. Or 0.9+ F1 across 10+ detection modules. Pick one, tell it precisely with numbers.

qs.q: How do you handle disagreements about model design with teammates?
qs.a:
Separate disagreements about opinions from disagreements about facts. Most ML disagreements are empirical - test both approaches.

Process:

  1. Understand their position first: "Help me understand why you prefer X" - collect reasoning, don't argue
  2. Agree on success criteria before debating: what metric determines who's right?
  3. Run both experiments if feasible: a 2-hour ablation study resolves more than a 2-hour debate
  4. Opinion only: defer to whoever has more relevant domain experience, or whoever will implement it
  5. Document the decision and reasoning for future revisit if results diverge

Avoid: ego-driven disagreements, HiPPO effect (Highest Paid Person's Opinion wins), deciding without data when data is available.

qs.q: Describe your experience teaching AI. What's the hardest concept to explain?
qs.a:
Use concrete examples from InterviewReady (200+ engineers) and TensorTonic (30k+ sign-ups).

Hard concepts (pick one you actually struggled to teach):

  • Backpropagation: the chain rule is easy; why we can compute all gradients in one backward pass is hard. Key insight: they are computing a product of Jacobians with memoization - O(forward pass).
  • KV cache: most engineers understand caching. Specific confusion: why cache K and V but not Q? Q is the "question" for the current new token; K and V are history we reuse.
  • RLHF vs DPO: engineers understand supervised learning, not RL. Insight: DPO replaces the RL loop with a direct supervised objective derived from the RLHF optimal policy - alignment without RL training.

interview angle: mention specific misconceptions students had. Shows pedagogical depth beyond just knowing the content.

qs.q: What interests you specifically about this company's work? (Prepare per company.)
qs.a:
Generic answers fail here. Prepare something specific enough it couldn't apply to any other company.

Per company:

  • OpenAI: o3/o4 reasoning models, Whisper, Operator (agents). "I find the o3 approach - scaling verification rather than generation - more interesting than pure scale."
  • Anthropic: safety + interpretability research. "The dictionary-learning work (Towards / Scaling Monosemanticity) made me curious about what circuits Claude learns for reasoning."
  • Google DeepMind: AlphaFold, Gemini, robotics. "Gemini's million-token context and what it takes to train and serve it."
  • Meta AI: LLaMA open ecosystem, SAM, DINO. "Meta open-sourcing frontier models changes the entire research ecosystem - democratizes alignment research."
  • Sarvam AI: "The challenge of high-quality ASR for code-switched speech across 22 Indian languages with limited labeled data."
  • Krutrim: "Building India's sovereign AI stack - multilingual tokenization and culturally-grounded pretraining for Indian languages."

qs.q: Where do you see the AI field heading in the next 3 years?
qs.a:
Tests intellectual engagement with the field. Give a genuine opinion, then defend it.

Strong view areas (pick 1-2 and go deep):

  • Reasoning and verification: the o1/o3 paradigm - scaling compute at inference via "thinking" separates capability tiers. Models that verify their own outputs become more reliable than those that don't.
  • Agentic systems: LLMs will run entire software development workflows, not just assist. Bottleneck moves from model capability to reliable long-horizon tool use.
  • On-device intelligence: 7B models on laptops and phones, enabled by quantization + mobile hardware. Privacy-preserving AI becomes practical at scale.
  • Multimodal natively: models trained jointly on text, image, audio, video, code from scratch - not modality bolted on.

Be honest: "I don't know" is acceptable for specific timelines. A genuinely held view beats a diplomatic non-answer. Karpathy's insight: progress is fast but reliability and safety lag capability by years.

qs.q: Tell me about a time you made a decision with incomplete data.
qs.a:
Tests comfort with uncertainty and decision-making under ambiguity - core skill at startups and research labs.

STAR for ML context:

  • Situation: goal, timeline, why data was incomplete
  • Task: what decision needed to be made? Stakes?
  • Action: how did you quantify uncertainty? What assumptions did you make explicit? Did you prioritize getting more data vs. acting with what you had?
  • Result: what happened? Was the decision vindicated? What would you do differently?

Key insight to demonstrate: you make uncertainty explicit (confidence intervals, sensitivity analysis) rather than pretending more confidence than the data supports. Show you can act despite uncertainty, not just analyze it.

qs.q: How do you measure ROI of an AI feature?
qs.a:
Measures business acumen + ML engineering maturity. Pure ML engineers skip this; strong candidates think end-to-end.

Framework:

  1. Baseline cost: what does the non-AI solution cost? (human labor, rule engine, or no solution at all)
  2. AI solution cost: compute (inference cost), human review, maintenance overhead, annotation cost
  3. Value: what metric does the AI feature move?
    • Fraud detection: TPR improvement × avg fraud value × transactions = annual savings
    • Recommendation: A/B test CTR lift × monetization per click × traffic = revenue
    • Automation: tasks/hour × human cost/hour = labor savings
  4. Payback period: when does cumulative value exceed development + operating cost?

Gotcha: include model maintenance and retraining costs. Most ROI calculations omit this and underestimate total cost.

qs.q: A PM wants 90% accuracy but the model achieves 82%. What do you do?
qs.a:
This is about requirements negotiation, not just model improvement.

Step 1: understand where 90% came from. Business requirement (need to replace current process)? Or round number someone invented? Very different problems.

Step 2: challenge the metric. Is accuracy right? With class imbalance, 82% accuracy might be 0.3 F1. 82% at high precision might beat 90% at lower precision depending on the cost structure.

Step 3: price the gap. "Going from 82% to 90% requires 10× more labeled data, 3 months, possibly a different architecture, and may not be achievable given label noise. Here's what 85% costs for 2 weeks."

Step 4: propose alternatives. Confidence thresholding: achieve 92% accuracy on 70% of cases (high-confidence), route remaining 30% to humans. System-level accuracy meets the 90% bar.

The right answer is not "I'll improve the model." It's a business/engineering conversation first.

qs.q: Tell me about a time you pushed back on a technical direction and were wrong. What did you learn?
qs.a:
This question tests intellectual honesty and how you update beliefs under evidence - arguably more important in ML than in most engineering domains because ML involves constant uncertainty.

What interviewers want to hear:

  • You had a clear technical opinion and stated it (not passive)
  • You were genuinely wrong, not just deferring to authority
  • You updated the view based on evidence (data, results, a colleague's reasoning)
  • You extracted a durable lesson, not just "I was wrong once"

Structure: situation → the position → counter-evidence you encountered → how you changed course → what you now look for before pushing back on similar decisions.

Trap to avoid: picking a story where you were "wrong" but actually right, or where the stakes were trivially low. The question is a calibration check - interviewers (especially at Anthropic, DeepMind) will probe whether you are genuinely intellectually honest or performing humility.

qs.q: Tell me about a production incident in a live camera system. How did you find it, fix it, and stop it from recurring?
qs.a:
This tests on-call judgment and whether you think in systems. Use a real incident; interviewers probe details quickly.

Structure:

  1. Detection: how you learned about it (monitor, customer, operator) and how long that took. If a customer told you, say so and say what monitor you added.
  2. Blast radius: how many cameras or sites, which alerts were wrong or missing, for how long.
  3. Mitigation before root cause: what you did in the first hour to stop the damage (rollback, raise a threshold on one site, disable a rule) and why that was safe.
  4. Diagnosis: the hypotheses you ruled out with evidence, in order. Name the tools (logs, replayed streams, per-camera metrics).
  5. Root cause and fix.
  6. Prevention: the check, test, alert or release gate you added, and whether it has caught anything since.

Prepare before the interview: the timeline with real numbers (cameras affected, hours, alert counts), what you would do differently, and one thing you got wrong during the response.

Avoid: blaming another team, a story with no measurement, or a fix that was only "we were more careful".

qs.q: You own models running on hundreds of cameras and every site has a complaint. How do you decide what to work on?
qs.a:
This tests prioritisation under noise. Show a method, then one example.

Method:

  • Quantify each issue in one shared unit: false alerts/day or missed events/day × cameras affected × cost per error. A complaint from the loudest site is a data point, not a ranking.
  • Group by root cause: 40 complaints often collapse into 3 causes (night IR mode, one camera model, a threshold). Fix causes, not tickets.
  • Separate fix types by cost: config (threshold, ROI, debounce) takes hours; data plus retrain takes weeks; architecture change takes months. Ship cheap fixes for the big buckets first, and start the slow fix for the largest bucket in parallel.
  • Protect fleet health: anything that can break all cameras (release process, monitoring gaps) outranks a single-site accuracy issue.
  • Say no explicitly: tell the sites you deprioritised what you are doing instead and when you will revisit.

Strong signal: you built the measurement that made prioritisation possible (per-camera alert dashboards, a labeled sample per site) rather than prioritising by intuition.
